title: The Second Run Down the Mountain
author: Morgan Housel
wiifm: You run businesses that live and die on other people's money decisions: loans, debts, repayments, risk. Morgan Housel's argument is that those decisions are rarely made on a spreadsheet. They are made at a dinner table, shaped by fear, ego and whatever the economy was doing when someone was young. You will follow Housel from a ski slope in California where luck decided who lived, through a hotel car park full of Ferraris, to a quiet book about why ordinary behaviour beats brilliance. You will come out with a calmer, more durable way of thinking about your own money.

b: Morgan Housel grew up skiing around Lake Tahoe in California, and in his late teens he raced for the Squaw Valley ski team. His closest friends were teammates. In February 2001 a warm storm dumped about three feet of heavy, wet snow on top of the lighter powder that had fallen before it. Housel later wrote that heavy snow on fluffy snow is textbook avalanche conditions.

On the twenty-first of February, he and two friends, Brendan Allan and Bryan Richmond, ducked out of the patrolled resort to ski the backside of a mountain called KT-22, a long stretch of untouched slope between Squaw Valley and the neighbouring Alpine Meadows. On the first run a small slide caught Housel. They made it down, hitchhiked back, and his friends wanted to go again.

Housel did not. He has said he cannot really explain why. Partly he disliked hitchhiking. So he offered to drive round to the back-country road and pick them up at the bottom. He waited. They never came. That evening he searched with a friend, the police were called, and rescuers went up after midnight to find a vast avalanche field. The next morning dogs and probes found Brendan and Bryan buried under about six feet of snow.

Housel tells this story not as a lesson about skiing but as a lesson about risk and luck. The same decision, made by the same three boys, produced utterly different outcomes, and the difference had nothing to do with skill. That idea sits under everything he went on to write about money.
ch.cap: Housel waits by the car as the slope lets go

b: After school Housel studied finance at the University of Southern California, and to make money he worked as a valet at a luxury hotel in Los Angeles. He parked Ferraris, Lamborghinis and Rolls-Royces all day. He dreamed of owning one, because he assumed that a man in a car like that would be admired.

It took him years to notice something about his own behaviour. When a gleaming Ferrari pulled in, he never once looked at the driver and thought, what a cool guy. He thought, if I had that car, people would think I was cool. He calls this the man in the car paradox. People want wealth partly to signal that they should be liked and admired, but other people rarely admire the person. They use the car to imagine themselves being admired.

Many of the drivers, he later learned, were not rich at all. Some were heavily in debt or simply renting the car. This is one of the quiet traps of money. We see what people spend, not what they have. Wealth is what you do not see: the car not bought, the extension not built, the money left invested. A big house is visible. A large pension is invisible. So we learn from the wrong examples.

Housel's point is not that you should never buy nice things. It is that you should know why you are buying them. If you want respect and admiration, he suggests, humility, kindness and empathy will win you far more of it than horsepower ever will.
ch.cap: The young valet dreams of himself in the Ferrari

b: Housel began writing about finance just as the financial system was falling apart. In 2008 he joined The Motley Fool, the investment website, and spent the next years writing about markets, the crash and the long recovery. Later he wrote a column for The Wall Street Journal, and in 2016 he joined Collaborative Fund, a venture capital firm, as a partner, writing on its blog.

Watching 2008 at close quarters taught him something that the textbooks underplayed. Smart, highly paid, highly qualified people had made catastrophic decisions. The problem was rarely knowledge. It was behaviour. And the behaviour of each person made sense from inside their own life.

This became the opening argument of his book. Nobody is crazy, he wrote. Someone who grew up during high inflation in the 1970s thinks about savings differently from someone who grew up during the long boom of the 1990s. Research by the economists Ulrike Malmendier and Stefan Nagel found that people's willingness to invest in shares is shaped by the returns they personally lived through in their early adult years. Your experience of money is a tiny sample of what can happen, but it feels like the whole truth.

He also points out how new all of this is. Widespread retirement saving, index funds and personal credit on today's scale are only a few decades old. We are all, in a sense, amateurs, improvising with tools our grandparents did not have.

So when someone makes a money decision that looks foolish from the outside, a lottery ticket bought on a low income, a loan taken on terms you would never accept, Housel asks you to pause. To the person making it, it is probably the most sensible choice available given what they have seen and what they fear. Understanding that is the beginning of helping them.
ch.cap: Housel writes through the night as 2008 crashes

ch.h: The friend who died on the mountain
b: The avalanche gave Housel a lifelong respect for luck, and he found the same lesson in the most famous success story in business. In the late 1960s, Lakeside School in Seattle was one of very few schools in the world with access to a computer terminal. A pupil named Bill Gates got to use it. Housel notes that the odds of that access were tiny, and that without it Microsoft might never have existed.

But Gates had a best friend at Lakeside, Kent Evans, who was by Gates's own account as gifted as he was and just as obsessed with computers. They planned to build things together. In 1972, before he graduated, Kent Evans died in a mountaineering accident. Housel calls Kent the counterweight to Bill. For every Gates whose luck went right, there is a Kent Evans whose luck went wrong, and we never hear about him.

The point is not that success is all luck. It is that luck and risk are siblings: the same force that lifts some people flattens others, and neither is fully explained by effort. So be careful whom you praise and whom you look down on. And when you judge your own results, focus less on individual cases and more on broad patterns.

Housel turns this into a working rule. When things are going well for you, assume that some of it is luck and do not stretch yourself on the belief that you are a genius. When things go badly, forgive yourself a little, because some of that is luck too. And when you study other people, look for the patterns that repeat across many lives rather than the single dazzling exception.
ch.cap: Bill Gates and Kent Evans at the Lakeside terminal

b: Housel's favourite pair of stories involves two men who never met. Ronald Read was a petrol station attendant and later a janitor in Brattleboro, Vermont. When he died in 2014, aged ninety-two, his neighbours learned he had an estate of about eight million dollars, most of it left to the local hospital and library. He had simply saved what he could and bought shares in large, sturdy companies, and held them for decades.

Richard Fuscone, by contrast, was a Harvard-educated former executive at Merrill Lynch who retired early to do philanthropic work. He borrowed heavily to build an enormous house in Connecticut. When the financial crisis hit in 2008, he was overextended, and in the following years he declared personal bankruptcy.

There is no other field, Housel says, where a janitor can beat a highly educated professional. It cannot happen in surgery or in bridge-building. It happens in money because finance is less about what you know and more about how you behave. Patience, humility and frugality can beat intelligence, and greed or leverage can wreck it.

Housel's own conclusion is that the most powerful thing in Read's life was not stock picking. It was time, combined with the simple habit of not interrupting it. Read lived modestly, chopped his own firewood, and let decades of ordinary returns compound into something extraordinary.
ch.cap: The janitor chops firewood; the banker's mansion cracks

b: One of the darkest chapters is about enough. Housel tells of Rajat Gupta, who rose from an orphaned childhood in India to run the consultancy McKinsey and become extremely wealthy. It was not sufficient. He wanted to be a billionaire, and he passed inside information from the board of Goldman Sachs to the hedge fund manager Raj Rajaratnam. Gupta was convicted of insider trading in 2012 and went to prison.

Housel puts it bluntly: the hardest financial skill is getting the goalpost to stop moving. If expectations rise with results, there is no logic in striving for more, because you will feel the same after putting in more effort. Some things, he argues, are never worth risking for more money: reputation, freedom, family, being loved by those you want to love you, and happiness.

He makes the same point with the history of ice ages. Geologists long puzzled over how the earth froze, and the answer turned out to be not brutal winters but slightly cool summers. A little snow failed to melt each year, the white surface reflected more sunlight, and the cooling compounded over thousands of years until ice sheets covered continents. Small, steady effects, given enough time, become enormous. Compounding is not intuitive, Housel argues, which is why people constantly underestimate it and keep reaching for big, risky returns instead.

He links this to the investor Warren Buffett, and makes a striking calculation. By Housel's figures, almost all of Buffett's wealth was accumulated after he turned sixty-five. Buffett is a fine investor, but the secret to his fortune is time. He began in childhood and never stopped. Compounding rewards whoever survives longest, which is why the most important goal is not to be ruined along the way.
ch.cap: An old man rolls a snowball that keeps on growing

b: Housel draws a hard line between two skills that look like one. Getting money requires taking risks, being optimistic and putting yourself out there. Keeping money requires the opposite: frugality, humility and a healthy fear that what you have built could be taken away just as fast.

His illustration is from October 1929, when the American stock market collapsed. A trader named Jesse Livermore had bet against the market and, by the usual estimate, made around one hundred million dollars in the crash, one of the greatest trading coups in history. Success made him bolder. He took larger and larger positions, borrowed heavily and lost almost everything within a few years. He died by suicide in 1940.

In the same week of 1929, according to a short report in The New York Times, a Manhattan property developer called Abraham Germansky, who had borrowed heavily to buy shares, was reported missing by his wife after the crash. Housel sets the two stories side by side to show that a single market event can make or break anyone who has stopped thinking about survival.

So he recommends a curious combination: be optimistic about the long run and paranoid about the short run. Expect things to get better over decades, and arrange your affairs so that you can get through the ugly years in between without being forced to sell, borrow or give up.
ch.cap: October 1929: one trader wins big, another vanishes

b: From survival comes the most practical idea in the book: margin of safety. Plan for things not to go to plan. Housel's view is that saving, even without a specific purpose, is a hedge against life's ability to surprise you at the worst moment. Cash in the bank is not wasted. It is freedom, the ability to say no to a bad deal, a bad boss or a bad month.

He calls control over your time the highest dividend money pays. Being able to wake up and say, I can do whatever I want today, makes people happier than almost any purchase. Most of what wealth buys, he argues, is not things but options.

He separates rich from wealthy. Rich is current income: the car, the watch, the visible signs. Wealthy is the money you have not spent, sitting quietly and growing. He also admits his own household's choices are not perfectly rational. He and his wife paid off their mortgage, which a spreadsheet might say was a mistake when borrowing was cheap. He did it anyway, because the feeling of independence was worth more to him than the extra return. His advice is to be reasonable rather than coldly rational, and choose a plan you can actually stick with when things go wrong.

He applies the same humility to forecasting. History, he notes, is the study of change, and its greatest events, the Great Depression, the September the eleventh attacks, a global pandemic, were by definition unprecedented when they happened. So the worst case in your plan should not be the worst thing that has happened before. It should leave room for something worse.
ch.cap: Mortgage paid, the household stays warm through the storm

b: Housel's last big idea is about tails, the rare extreme outcomes that dominate results. In venture capital, most investments fail and a tiny handful make all the money. Across the history of the stock market, a small proportion of companies account for most of the gains. Walt Disney made hundreds of cartoons, many of which lost money, before Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs in 1937 transformed his company.

The lesson is that you can be wrong half the time and still do very well, if the few things you get right are big enough and you stay in the game long enough for them to arrive. Volatility, the sickening drops in markets and businesses, is not a fine for doing something wrong. It is the fee for being there. People who treat it as a fine try to dodge it and usually miss the gains.

The Psychology of Money was published in September 2020, in the middle of a pandemic, and sold millions of copies around the world. It is a short, gentle book, built from blog posts, and economists would say little in it is new. Housel would agree. His claim is not originality but emphasis: the soft skills matter more than the technical ones.
And underneath, still, is that mountain. Two friends went up and one did not. He never claimed to understand why. He built a philosophy on accepting that we cannot.
ch.cap: Hundreds of cartoons, then one golden reel in 1937

take: People's money choices are shaped by what they lived through. Before judging a client's decisions, ask what their experience of money has been.
For every Bill Gates there is a Kent Evans. Do not copy individual success stories wholesale, and do not condemn individual failures too fast.
If your wants rise as fast as your results, you will never feel richer. Decide what enough looks like and protect it.
Compounding rewards whoever stays in the game longest. Avoid any risk, such as heavy borrowing, that could knock you out completely.
Plan for things not to go to plan. Keep a cash buffer in the business and at home so a bad month does not become a crisis.
Control over your own time is the highest dividend money pays. Spend on freedom before spending on things others will see.
Wealth is what you do not see
Visible spending is not wealth. Judge financial health by what is saved and kept, not by cars and houses.
Drops in markets and businesses are the price of the long-run gain, not a punishment. Pay it calmly rather than bailing out.
recall: What happened on the mountain in February 2001?

Housel and two friends skied out of bounds on the backside of KT-22 near Squaw Valley. Housel declined a second run and his friends Brendan Allan and Bryan Richmond were killed in an avalanche. He uses it to show how luck and risk shape outcomes regardless of skill.
What is the man in the car paradox?

People want expensive things to be admired, but observers rarely admire the owner. They imagine themselves owning the thing instead. So spending for status mostly fails to win the respect it was meant to buy.
Why could Ronald Read beat Richard Fuscone?

Read, a janitor, saved patiently and held shares for decades, leaving about eight million dollars. Fuscone, a Merrill Lynch executive, borrowed heavily and went bankrupt after 2008. Behaviour mattered more than knowledge or income.
What is the point of the Kent Evans story?

Kent was Bill Gates's equally gifted friend at Lakeside School, who died in a mountaineering accident before graduating. He shows that the same luck and risk that made Gates also destroyed someone else, so outcomes are poor guides to skill.
What is Housel's view of being rational?

He suggests aiming to be reasonable rather than coldly rational. A plan you can stick with through bad times, like his own choice to pay off his mortgage, can beat a technically better plan you will abandon.
note: The avalanche account follows Housel's own essay The Three Sides of Risk on the Collaborative Fund blog, which dates it to 21 February 2001. Ronald Read, Kent Evans, Rajat Gupta, Jesse Livermore and the Lakeside terminal are documented in public sources; Livermore's crash profit is a commonly cited estimate rather than an audited figure. Fuscone's story comes from news reports of his bankruptcy. The book synthesises existing research and blog essays rather than offering new scholarship, and its Buffett figures are Housel's own calculations.

The habit of living well below your means and avoiding waste.

The error of learning only from the winners we can see while ignoring the many who failed and vanished from view.

stories: The second run he did not take

biz: Build the embankment before the bad month

Housel's rule is optimism about the long run and paranoia about the short run. Ruby Holdings depends on things it does not control: ad platform policies, lender appetite and FCA rules. This week, work out how many months of fixed costs the business could cover with zero leads, and set a target, say six. List how much commission comes from the single biggest lender and the single biggest ad channel. If either is above half, plan a second source. And do not raise fixed spending on the back of one strong month, which may be luck.
Nobody is crazy, including the client

Housel says every money decision makes sense from inside the life that made it. Debt Support Direct clients often arrive ashamed of choices that look reckless from outside. Train advisers to ask what led to each debt before discussing solutions, and to reflect back what the client was trying to protect. For HomeownersLoan, the same curiosity matters before consolidating unsecured debt into a loan secured on the home, because the client must understand the added risk and longer term costs. Measure it through call reviews: how often did the adviser ask why before telling what?
connects: Taleb's Black Swan shares Housel's claim that rare extreme events, the tails, dominate outcomes and that plans must survive the unprecedented.
Seneca, one of the richest men in Rome, wrote to Lucilius that the person who has enough is rich, Housel's goalpost that stops moving.
Munger, like Housel, prized patience, avoiding ruin and letting compounding work uninterrupted over decades.
recap:
In February two thousand and one, three teenage ski racers sneaked out of a resort near Lake Tahoe to ski fresh snow. A small slide caught one of them, Morgan Housel, on the first run. His friends wanted to go again. Housel did not, and he still cannot say why. He drove round to collect them at the bottom. They never arrived. Rescuers found them under an avalanche the next morning.

The same decision, by the same boys, had opposite outcomes, and skill had nothing to do with it. That is the first big idea of The Psychology of Money. Luck and risk are siblings. For every Bill Gates who had rare access to a school computer, there is a Kent Evans, his equally gifted best friend, killed on a mountain at seventeen. So be humble about your wins, forgiving about your losses, and learn from patterns, not dazzling exceptions.

Housel studied finance, parked Ferraris as a hotel valet, and began writing about money in two thousand and eight, just as the financial system collapsed. He saw clever people make terrible choices. His second idea is that nobody is crazy. Each of us learns about money from our own small slice of history, and our decisions make sense from inside our own lives.

The third idea is that behaviour beats intelligence. Ronald Read, a petrol attendant and janitor in Vermont, quietly saved and held good shares for decades and left about eight million dollars. Richard Fuscone, a Harvard educated banker, borrowed heavily for a huge house and went bankrupt. In no other field can a janitor beat a professional. Patience and time did the work. By Housel's figures, almost all of Warren Buffett's fortune arrived after he turned sixty five, because compounding rewards whoever survives longest.

That leads to the fourth idea. Getting rich and staying rich are different skills. Jesse Livermore made a fortune in the crash of nineteen twenty nine, grew bolder, borrowed, and lost almost everything. So be optimistic about the long run and paranoid about the short run. Leave room for error. Save without a reason. The highest dividend money pays is control over your own time.

The fifth idea is enough. The hardest skill is getting the goalpost to stop moving, because some things, your reputation, your freedom, your family, are never worth risking for more.

Underneath it all is still that mountain. Two friends went up, and one did not, and Housel built a philosophy on accepting that he will never know why.

The line to remember: wealth is what you do not see.
